title: Lightning could strike more than twice as often in a warming world
summary: Besides fires and floods, droughts and storms, another type of extreme weather may be getting more common due to climate change: lightning. Globally, in a future of high greenhouse gas emissions, lightning may get 76% to 140% more common by the end of the century than between 1995 and 2014, according to a new study published in Earth's Future.

Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked peer-reviewed publication trusted source proofread The GIST Add to Preferred Sources Credit: Unsplash/CC0 Public Domain Besides fires and floods, droughts and storms, another type of extreme weather may be getting more common due to climate change: lightning. Globally, in a future of high greenhouse gas emissions, lightning may get 76% to 140% more common by the end of the century than between 1995 and 2014, according to a new study published in Earth's Future . The projections apply specifically to "cloud-to-ground lightning"—the dangerous bolts that touch down to Earth, sparking wildfires and damaging wind turbines, power lines, offshore oil rigs and other infrastructure. Cloud-to-ground lightning kills several thousand humans and hundreds of millions of trees around the world each year. A dance of heat and ice "There is actually quite a large uncertainty about how lightning will respond to climate change," said Andreas Krause, an Earth system scientist at the Technical University of Munich and lead author of the study. That's because the genesis of lightning depends on both heat and cold. When air near Earth's surface warms up, it rises (a process known as convection), stirring the cold atmosphere above. In the turbulence, tiny ice crystals in the frigid mid-atmosphere clouds jostle and collide, exchanging electric charge. Eventually, the lighter crystals loft upward relative to the larger, heavier ones, carrying their different charges in opposite directions and creating an electric field. Once that field gets big enough, ZAP!—lightning is born. As climate change raises air temperatures around the globe, more convection stirs up the clouds, potentially generating more lightning. We already see a version of this in existing lightning patterns, Krause noted: Lightning peaks in the early afternoon, when it's typically hottest, and strikes more often in the warm tropics than in the colder high latitudes. But warmer air could also mean fewer ice crystals high up in the atmosphere, making it harder for strong electric fields—and, by extension, lightning itself—to form. "It's not quite clear which of these is more important," Krause said. Lightning amping up To predict densities of cloud-to-ground lightning under different climate conditions, the team trained a machine learning model with lightning and climate observations from 2019 that included temperature, rainfall, humidity, air pressure, wind speed and incoming radiation from the sun. Applied to the climate conditions of 1901 to 1920 and 1995 to 2014, the model indicated that the frequency of cloud-to-ground lightning rose 11% over the 20th century—equivalent to about 12% for every degree Celsius of warming. But under a high-emissions future (corresponding to the SSP3-7.0 scenario), that relationship could become nearly three times as sensitive, bumping up lightning frequency by 30% for each degree of warming. This would mean that, compared to the conditions of 1995 to 2014, ground-striking lightning would get 76% to 140% more common by the end of this century, depending on the climate model projections considered. Those numbers far outstrip previous estimates, the highest of which project cloud-to-ground lightning frequency rising between 8% and 17% per degree of warming. The discrepancy stems mostly from different mathematical approaches to estimate future lightning frequency and the new study's use of a newer, more robust global lightning data set. "I was quite surprised that the projections were so high," Krause said. "I expected smaller changes."
